name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q01 - Respiratory organs across different animal groups

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms in List I with their respective respiratory structures in List II:

List I (Organisms)List II (Respiratory Structures)
(A) Earthworm(I) Network of tracheal tubes
(B) Aquatic arthropods(II) Entire body surface
(C) Lower invertebrates (Sponges)(III) Moist cuticle
(D) Insects(IV) Gills

Select the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the respiratory structures of lower invertebrates.
Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide by simple diffusion across their entire body surface.

Step 2: Analyze the respiratory mechanism of earthworms.
Earthworms utilize their moist cuticle for cutaneous exchange of respiratory gases.

Step 3: Analyze the respiratory mechanism of aquatic arthropods.
Aquatic arthropods, such as prawns, possess specialized vascularized structures called gills (branchial respiration) for gaseous exchange.

Step 4: Analyze the respiratory mechanism of insects.
Insects utilize an extensive network of tracheal tubes that conduct atmospheric air directly to body tissues.

Step 5: Formulate the matching pairs and final answer.
Earthworm pairs with Moist cuticle (A-III); Aquatic arthropods pair with Gills (B-IV); Lower invertebrates pair with Entire body surface (C-II); Insects pair with Network of tracheal tubes (D-I). The correct combination is A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I.

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory volumes listed in List I with their typical physiological values in List II:

List I (Respiratory Volume)List II (Typical Volume)
(A) Tidal Volume (TV)(I) \(1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL}\)
(B) Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)(II) \(1100\text{ mL to }1200\text{ mL}\)
(C) Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)(III) \(500\text{ mL}\)
(D) Residual Volume (RV)(IV) \(2500\text{ mL to }3000\text{ mL}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Tidal Volume (TV).
Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal respiration, which is approximately \(500\text{ mL}\).

Step 2: Identify Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV).
IRV is the additional volume of air a person can inspire by a forcible inspiration, averaging \(2500\text{ mL to }3000\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: Identify Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV).
ERV is the additional volume of air a person can expire by a forcible expiration, averaging \(1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL}\).

Step 4: Identify Residual Volume (RV).
RV is the volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration, averaging \(1100\text{ mL to }1200\text{ mL}\).

Step 5: Correlate the pairs to determine the final match.
The correct association is Tidal Volume with \(500\text{ mL}\) (A-III), Inspiratory Reserve Volume with \(2500\text{ mL to }3000\text{ mL}\) (B-IV), Expiratory Reserve Volume with \(1000\text{ mL to }1100\text{ mL}\) (C-I), and Residual Volume with \(1100\text{ mL to }1200\text{ mL}\) (D-II). The correct sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q03 - Pulmonary capacities and derived volume combinations

questiontext.text:
Match the pulmonary capacities in List I with their corresponding constituent volumes in List II:

List I (Pulmonary Capacity)List II (Constituent Volumes)
(A) Inspiratory Capacity (IC)(I) \(\text{ERV} + \text{RV}\)
(B) Expiratory Capacity (EC)(II) \(\text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\)
(C) Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)(III) \(\text{TV} + \text{IRV}\)
(D) Vital Capacity (VC)(IV) \(\text{TV} + \text{ERV}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define Inspiratory Capacity.
Inspiratory capacity is the total volume of air a person can inspire after a normal expiration; it includes Tidal Volume and Inspiratory Reserve Volume (\(\text{TV} + \text{IRV}\)).

Step 2: Define Expiratory Capacity.
Expiratory capacity is the total volume of air a person can expire after a normal inspiration; it includes Tidal Volume and Expiratory Reserve Volume (\(\text{TV} + \text{ERV}\)).

Step 3: Define Functional Residual Capacity.
Functional residual capacity is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration; it consists of Expiratory Reserve Volume and Residual Volume (\(\text{ERV} + \text{RV}\)).

Step 4: Define Vital Capacity.
Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or breathe out after a forced inspiration); it encompasses \(\text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\).

Step 5: Identify the final matched combination.
The correct match pairs Inspiratory Capacity with \(\text{TV} + \text{IRV}\) (A-III), Expiratory Capacity with \(\text{TV} + \text{ERV}\) (B-IV), Functional Residual Capacity with \(\text{ERV} + \text{RV}\) (C-I), and Vital Capacity with \(\text{ERV} + \text{TV} + \text{IRV}\) (D-II). The matching sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q04 - Partial pressures of oxygen across anatomical compartments

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical sites or compartments in List I with the corresponding partial pressure of oxygen (\(\text{pO}_2\)) in List II:

List I (Site / Compartment)List II (\(\text{pO}_2\text{ in mm Hg}\))
(A) Atmospheric air(I) \(40\)
(B) Alveoli(II) \(95\)
(C) Deoxygenated blood(III) \(159\)
(D) Oxygenated blood(IV) \(104\)

Select the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the partial pressure of oxygen in atmospheric air.
In atmospheric air at sea level, oxygen accounts for a partial pressure (\(\text{pO}_2\)) of \(159\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 2: Determine \(\text{pO}_2\) in the alveoli.
In alveolar air, due to humidification and continuous gas exchange, \(\text{pO}_2\) is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 3: Determine \(\text{pO}_2\) in deoxygenated blood.
In deoxygenated systemic venous blood returning to the heart and entering pulmonary arteries, \(\text{pO}_2\) is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 4: Determine \(\text{pO}_2\) in oxygenated blood.
In oxygenated blood leaving pulmonary capillaries and entering systemic arteries, \(\text{pO}_2\) reaches \(95\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 5: Formulate the final match.
Atmospheric air pairs with \(159\text{ mm Hg}\) (A-III); Alveoli pairs with \(104\text{ mm Hg}\) (B-IV); Deoxygenated blood pairs with \(40\text{ mm Hg}\) (C-I); Oxygenated blood pairs with \(95\text{ mm Hg}\) (D-II). The correct sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q05 - Partial pressures of carbon dioxide at different sites

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory compartments in List I with their corresponding partial pressures of carbon dioxide (\(\text{pCO}_2\)) in List II:

List I (Compartment)List II (\(\text{pCO}_2\text{ in mm Hg}\))
(A) Atmospheric air(I) \(45\)
(B) Alveoli(II) \(40\)
(C) Deoxygenated blood(III) \(0.3\)
(D) Tissues(IV) \(45\)

Choose the correct matching combination from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify \(\text{pCO}_2\) in atmospheric air.
Carbon dioxide is present in very low concentrations in the atmosphere, producing a \(\text{pCO}_2\) of \(0.3\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 2: Identify \(\text{pCO}_2\) in alveolar air.
In the alveoli, \(\text{pCO}_2\) is maintained at \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 3: Identify \(\text{pCO}_2\) in deoxygenated blood and tissues.
In metabolizing body tissues, catabolism generates carbon dioxide, maintaining a \(\text{pCO}_2\) of \(45\text{ mm Hg}\). As carbon dioxide diffuses into the systemic capillaries, deoxygenated blood also carries a \(\text{pCO}_2\) of \(45\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 4: Establish the corresponding pairs.
Atmospheric air corresponds to \(0.3\text{ mm Hg}\) (A-III); Alveoli corresponds to \(40\text{ mm Hg}\) (B-II); Deoxygenated blood corresponds to \(45\text{ mm Hg}\) (C-I); Tissues corresponds to \(45\text{ mm Hg}\) (D-IV). The correct matching arrangement is A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q06 - Anatomical structures of human respiratory tract

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical structures in List I with their descriptions or characteristics in List II:

List I (Anatomical Structure)List II (Description / Characteristic)
(A) Epiglottis(I) Divides into primary bronchi at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra
(B) Trachea(II) Thin elastic cartilaginous flap preventing entry of food into the larynx
(C) Pleural fluid(III) Cartilaginous box that aids in sound production
(D) Larynx(IV) Reduces friction between the double-layered pleural membranes

Select the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Correlate the structure and function of the epiglottis.
The epiglottis is a thin elastic cartilaginous flap that covers the glottis during swallowing to prevent the entry of food into the larynx.

Step 2: Correlate the anatomy of the trachea.
The trachea is a straight tube extending through the mid-thoracic cavity that divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.

Step 3: Correlate the role of pleural fluid.
Pleural fluid is situated between the outer and inner pleural membranes and acts to reduce friction on the lung surface during breathing movements.

Step 4: Correlate the function of the larynx.
The larynx is a cartilaginous box located at the opening of the trachea that produces sound, commonly called the sound box.

Step 5: Synthesize the final pairings.
Epiglottis pairs with Thin elastic cartilaginous flap (A-II); Trachea pairs with Divides at 5th thoracic vertebra (B-I); Pleural fluid pairs with Reduces friction (C-IV); Larynx pairs with Cartilaginous sound box (D-III). The correct match is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q07 - Respiratory neural and chemical regulatory centres

questiontext.text:
Match the regulatory centres or structures in List I with their anatomical locations and functions in List II:

List I (Regulatory Element)List II (Location and Function)
(A) Respiratory rhythm centre(I) Located in pons; reduces duration of inspiration and alters rate
(B) Pneumotaxic centre(II) Peripheral chemoreceptors recognizing changes in \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\)
(C) Central chemosensitive area(III) Located in medulla; primarily responsible for basic rhythm regulation
(D) Aortic arch and carotid artery receptors(IV) Situated adjacent to rhythm centre; activated by excess \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the role of the respiratory rhythm centre.
The respiratory rhythm centre is a specialized neural group located in the medulla oblongata that is primarily responsible for generating and maintaining the basal rhythm of respiration.

Step 2: Identify the role of the pneumotaxic centre.
The pneumotaxic centre is situated in the pons varolii; signals from this centre can reduce the duration of inspiration, thereby modulating the respiratory rate.

Step 3: Identify the role of the central chemosensitive area.
The central chemosensitive area lies adjacent to the rhythm centre in the medulla and is highly sensitive to increases in \(\text{CO}_2\) and hydrogen ion (\(\text{H}^+\)) concentrations.

Step 4: Identify the role of peripheral vascular receptors.
Receptors present in the aortic arch and carotid bodies detect arterial elevations in \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\) concentrations and relay corrective signals to the medulla rhythm centre.

Step 5: Compile the correct pairing sequence.
Respiratory rhythm centre pairs with Medulla centre responsible for rhythm (A-III); Pneumotaxic centre pairs with Pons centre altering inspiration duration (B-I); Central chemosensitive area pairs with Medulla region activated by \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}^+\) (C-IV); Aortic and carotid receptors pair with Peripheral chemoreceptors (D-II). The matching sequence is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

questiontext.text:
Match the respiratory conditions and disorders in List I with their primary clinical and pathological features in List II:

List I (Disorder)List II (Pathological Feature)
(A) Asthma(I) Proliferation of fibrous tissue leading to lung damage due to stone/dust grinding
(B) Emphysema(II) Inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles causing difficulty in breathing and wheezing
(C) Fibrosis(III) Damage to alveolar walls resulting in reduced respiratory exchange surface
(D) Cutaneous respiration(IV) Exchange of respiratory gases through moist skin as seen in amphibians

Select the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the clinical pathology of asthma.
Asthma is characterized by wheezing and dyspnea due to allergic inflammation and bronchospasm of the bronchi and bronchioles.

Step 2: Understand the pathological mechanism of emphysema.
Emphysema is a chronic pulmonary disease, primarily caused by cigarette smoking, wherein the alveolar septa/walls are damaged, permanently reducing the total surface area available for gas exchange.

Step 3: Understand occupational fibrosis.
Occupational respiratory disorders arise in industries involving grinding or stone-breaking where chronic dust exposure overstimulates fibrous tissue proliferation (fibrosis), causing severe lung damage.

Step 4: Understand cutaneous respiration.
Cutaneous respiration is gas exchange occurring directly across vascularized, moist integument/skin, commonly observed in amphibians such as frogs.

Step 5: Determine the matching sequence.
Asthma pairs with Inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles (A-II); Emphysema pairs with Damage to alveolar walls decreasing respiratory surface (B-III); Fibrosis pairs with Proliferation of fibrous tissue from chronic dust exposure (C-I); Cutaneous respiration pairs with Exchange across moist skin (D-IV). The correct matching arrangement is A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q09 - Quantitative transport forms of respiratory gases in blood

questiontext.text:
Match the transport modes of respiratory gases in blood in List I with their exact physiological proportions in List II:

List I (Mode of Gas Transport)List II (Proportion Transported)
(A) Oxygen transported by RBCs as oxyhaemoglobin(I) Nearly \(70\%\)
(B) Carbon dioxide transported as bicarbonate ion(II) Nearly \(20\text{ to }25\%\)
(C) Carbon dioxide carried as carbamino-haemoglobin(III) About \(97\%\)
(D) Carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma(IV) About \(7\%\)

Select the correct match from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the fractions of oxygen transport.
About \(97\%\) of oxygen is transported bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells as oxyhaemoglobin, whereas the remaining \(3\%\) is carried dissolved in blood plasma.

Step 2: Evaluate the major form of carbon dioxide transport.
Nearly \(70\%\) of carbon dioxide is transported in blood in the form of bicarbonate ions (\(\text{HCO}_3^-\)), facilitated by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase.

Step 3: Evaluate carbamino-haemoglobin transport.
Nearly \(20\text{ to }25\%\) of carbon dioxide is transported bound to the amine groups of haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin.

Step 4: Evaluate dissolved carbon dioxide in plasma.
About \(7\%\) of carbon dioxide is carried in a simple dissolved physical state within blood plasma.

Step 5: Deduce the matching sequence.
Oxygen by RBCs pairs with \(97\%\) (A-III); Carbon dioxide as bicarbonate pairs with \(70\%\) (B-I); Carbon dioxide as carbamino-haemoglobin pairs with \(20\text{ to }25\%\) (C-II); Carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma pairs with \(7\%\) (D-IV). The correct matching sequence is A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MATCH_Q10 - Physiological factors governing haemoglobin oxygenation and delivery

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological parameters and delivery values in List I with their respective physiological states or values in List II:

List I (Physiological Condition / Process)List II (Characteristic / Quantitative Value)
(A) Conditions at alveolar surface favourable for oxyhaemoglobin formation(I) High \(\text{pCO}_2\), low \(\text{pO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\), higher temperature
(B) Conditions in active peripheral tissues causing oxygen dissociation(II) High \(\text{pO}_2\), low \(\text{pCO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\), lower temperature
(C) Volume of \(\text{O}_2\) delivered to tissues by \(100\text{ mL}\) oxygenated blood(III) Approximately \(4\text{ mL}\)
(D) Volume of \(\text{CO}_2\) delivered to alveoli by \(100\text{ mL}\) deoxygenated blood(IV) Approximately \(5\text{ mL}\)

Choose the correct matching arrangement from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze conditions favouring oxyhaemoglobin synthesis.
In the alveoli, the presence of high partial pressure of oxygen (\(\text{pO}_2\)), low partial pressure of carbon dioxide (\(\text{pCO}_2\)), lower hydrogen ion concentration (higher pH), and lower temperature shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left and promotes oxyhaemoglobin formation.

Step 2: Analyze conditions favouring oxygen dissociation at tissues.
In active metabolizing body tissues, low \(\text{pO}_2\), elevated \(\text{pCO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\) ion concentration, and higher temperature facilitate the release and dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.

Step 3: Quantify oxygen delivery to tissues.
Under resting physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated systemic arterial blood delivers approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of oxygen to the tissues.

Step 4: Quantify carbon dioxide delivery to alveoli.
Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood returning to pulmonary circulation delivers approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of carbon dioxide to the alveoli for expiration.

Step 5: Conclude the final match.
Conditions at alveolar surface match with High \(\text{pO}_2\), low \(\text{pCO}_2\), lesser \(\text{H}^+\), lower temperature (A-II); Conditions in tissues match with High \(\text{pCO}_2\), low \(\text{pO}_2\), high \(\text{H}^+\), higher temperature (B-I); Oxygen delivered per \(100\text{ mL}\) matches with \(5\text{ mL}\) (C-IV); Carbon dioxide delivered per \(100\text{ mL}\) matches with \(4\text{ mL}\) (D-III). The correct sequence is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
